claims.statement: Tom Allen said he would meet Charley Gallagher at any place Gallagher named, to draw up articles, if Gallagher covered the $200 deposit.
Tom Allen challenged Charley Gallagher to fight him for $500, apart from his McCoole match, in one day, one week or one month.
Tom Allen deposited $100 with his backer, Billy Carroll, at 510 Market Street, for Gallagher to cover.
On July 13, 1869, Tom Allen and Charley Gallagher made a match for $500 a side and the excursion money, to be fought on August 17 within fifty miles of St. Louis.
Ben Hogan arrived in St. Louis and said he was willing to fight Tom Allen.
Patsey Reardon published a challenge in a St. Louis paper to fight Tom Allen.
Tom Allen was already under engagement to fight McCoole when Gallagher asked for a meeting.
Jim Coyne challenged Ben Hogan to fight four weeks after the Allen and Gallagher fight, for $500 or $1,000 a side.
Charley Gallagher wanted to add about $1,000 to the stakes and fight Allen again after Allen and McCoole settled their dispute.
Joe Wormald wrote to Tom Allen asking him to arrange the preliminaries of a match with Ned O'Baldwin for $5,000 a side.
Allen accepted Gallagher's proposal to fight again for the same stakes, adding $1,000 a side.
Sherman Thurston said Allen had to fight McCoole before making any other engagement.
Tom Allen accepted Gallagher's proposal to leave the stakes on deposit and add $1,900 (printed as $1,900).
Allen would name a place within fifty miles of Cincinnati for the fight, to take place in a week or ten days.
Allen was to meet Gallagher at 3 o'clock on Saturday afternoon to draw up articles.
Jack Looney offered to back Charley Gallagher against Tom Allen for any amount once Gallagher recovered.
A deposit of $599 a side (printed as $599) for the Mike McCoole and Tom Allen match was to be made at Allen's saloon on the night of 9 October 1869.
$500 a side was put up for the Mike McCoole and Tom Allen match on the night of 9 October 1869.
Tom Allen said he was ready to fight Mike McCoole for the excursion money or for nothing, to settle which of them was superior.
A fight between Tom Allen and Mike McCoole was expected in November 1869, though doubtful.
Mike McCoole said he would fight Tom Allen only for the $5000 stakes, not for the excursion money.
Tom Allen was willing to fight McCoole for the excursion money or for anything, rather than let the match fall through.
Tom Allen and Mike McCoole were to fight for $5,000 and the championship of America on 10 November 1869, but the match fell through over a final stakeholder.
A telegram reported that Mace of London was matched to fight Tom Allen for $5,000 a side; Allen's friends and backers in St. Louis denied any such arrangement.
It is said that Tom Allen will not go back on his offer to accommodate any man in the world with a fight inside the ropes, but wants time for preliminaries.
The Clipper had reported that Jem Mace accepted Allen's challenge.
Tom Allen announced he would fight any man in America for $500 to $10,000, in a square stand-up fight under London prize ring rules.
Tom Allen offered to meet Joe Coburn in the ring anywhere in Wyoming Territory, whom he called the leading scientific pugilist in the United States.
Through Billy Carroll, Allen offered to fight Jem Mace for $2,500 a side, six months from signing articles.
Allen was ready to sign articles with Mace and put up a $500 forfeit (printed as $5€0), meeting between here and New York, about Pittsburgh.
Tom Allen apparently accepted Joe Coburn's challenge to fight for $10,000 (the report is garbled).
Tom Allen and Jem Mace each deposited $500 with a stakeholder last Saturday.
Jem Mace deposited $500 at the Clipper office to cover Tom Allen's challenge and asked Allen to cover it.
Mace would not meet Allen in Pittsburgh but offered to meet him in New York and pay half his expenses there.
Mace's New York friends proposed to present him with a belt, which he would stake against Allen's belt.
On Dec. 28, 1869, Tom Allen telegraphed that, not knowing Jem Mace's terms, he was not inclined to go to New York but would forward articles and a deposit.
Billy Carroll, acting for Tom Allen, forwarded forfeit money (printed as $690) to Frank Queen of the New York Clipper, accepting Mace's challenge.
